transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-22
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~55 minutes
Participants: Jordan Miles (Redwood AE), Priya Nambiar (Redwood SE), Marta Ruiz (Axion Head of ML), Devon Park (Axion Infra), Neil Ortiz (Axion PM)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect):
- Quick recap of pilot goals (chat summarization + retrieval + routing).
- Reviewed token economics: tokens/sec/$, cache hit savings, and batching tradeoffs.
- Bench run results: 12-15 tokens/sec per GPU baseline; with continuous prefix caching hit-rate 48% observed, effective tokens/sec/$ improved by ~1.9x in peak windows.
- Identified variance in sequence length distribution causing batching inefficiency; suggested short-term fixes and next steps for deeper on-prem testing.

Topics: pilot results, caching retention, batching policies, latency vs cost tradeoffs, security/SSO questions, next steps and action items.

[00:00] Jordan: okay, hi everyone, thanks for joining. Um quick roll call, we have Priya and I from Redwood, from Axion Marta, Devon, Neil?
[00:12] Marta: yeah hi, Marta here. thanks.
[00:14] Devon: Devon here.
[00:16] Neil: Neil on my side.
[00:18] Jordan: sweet, we're about 55 minutes scheduled, main goals—walk through the most recent pilot results you uploaded yesterday, talk caching experiments, and decide on the 2-hour retention test Priya proposed. Sound good?
[00:28] Marta: sounds perfect. Quick note, we're most worried about units per dollar and worst-case tail latency for customer-facing summarization.
[00:35] Priya: got it. I put a summary on the sheet but we'll run through it out loud.

[02:05] Priya: first slide, baseline numbers. We ran the 13B open model variant you requested on a single 80GB gpu instance. Raw token generation throughput averaged 13 tokens per second under synthetic steady-state load, variance +/- 2 tps. That maps to our hosted price unit of roughly 0.00012 $ per token when uncached — that's a rough mapping because your pilot has a reserved commit.
[02:35] Devon: wait, sorry, 13 tps is per GPU or per replica?
[02:38] Priya: per GPU single replica during the run. In multi-replica scaling we saw linear-ish scaling until we hit network queuing.
[02:46] Marta: and that's without any batching tuning?
[02:49] Priya: we had a default batch window of 12ms, dynamic continuous batching so it's not fully micro-batched. You requested low-latency so we kept small windows.

[05:00] Neil: the sheet includes a section labeled "KV cache" with an asterisk, I saw an overall 48% hit rate — is that real traffic or synthetic?
[05:09] Priya: real-ish; you sent a 24-hour sample of production requests last week, we replayed them with your retrieval prefix config. 48% is the overall hit-rate across the day, but it's spiky. In the morning peak we hit as high as 65% because more queries shared similar prefixes, mid-day dropped to 30% when ad-hoc long queries came in.
[05:28] Marta: that variance is my big worry — a single missed prefix causes tokens to blow up.

[07:10] Jordan: quick note on economics math—if baseline uncached tokens cost X, and you have hit-rate H, effective token count is X*(1-H) plus some small overhead for cache lookups; we estimate overhead at ~0.3-0.6% of token costs. So at 48% hit, you're roughly halving the token spend in sample windows. That drove the ~1.9x tokens/sec/$ improvement Priya mentioned.
[07:38] Devon: can you remind us of how we measured tokens/sec/$? I want to ensure it's apples-to-apples with our internal spreadsheet.
[07:44] Priya: sure — we take tokens generated per second per GPU divided by cost per second of that GPU under the pilot commit. So tokens/sec/$ = (tokens/sec) / (dollars/sec). You can convert to tokens per dollar by scaling. We included both in the sheet.

[09:55] Marta: what about latency — last week we saw spikes to 1.1s for short prompts even when cached; that's above our SLO of 500ms for interactive paths.
[10:05] Priya: correct; a few causes. One was network serialization on the host when the GPU was context switching heavy; another was cold cache misses which require rerun of the full forward pass. We're suggesting two mitigations: increase the cache retention window and proactive prefetch for top N prefixes, and second, tune batching window slightly upward during low interaction periods to increase throughput without materially increasing p95 in many cases.

[12:30] Devon: are we seeing anything related to quantization mismatch? I saw some noise in log where half-precision kernels spilled over under high token lengths.
[12:38] Priya: good question — our runtime used 4-bit quantization path for the model variant in the pilot. We did see slight variance in throughput when sequence length exceeded 1,024 tokens because some kernels fall back to slower paths. We capture that in the 'seq_len bucket' section of the sheet.

[14:10] Neil: so for our production use we probably need a mixed strategy: for interactive use keep a lower seq cap and heavier caching; for async batch jobs we can allow longer seqs and higher batching.
[14:20] Jordan: exactly; that's the smart routing idea we mentioned—route by latency target. Hosted for low-latency front-line, dedicated or private for heavy longer jobs.

[16:50] Marta: any security flags we should be tracking as we inch toward Private? SSO, audit logs, the usual.
[16:56] Jordan: yep, Redwood Private plan supports SAML SSO, audit trail, KMS integration — I will include the Private security checklist in the follow-up. We also have SOC 2 Type II and ISO documentation if needed for procurement.

[18:05] Priya: back to results — caching savings breakdown: at 48% hit-rate we saw effective token reduce by 45% once you account for KV lookup overhead and some reruns. The measurable cost per user session dropped from ~0.0126 USD to ~0.0069 USD in our test workload. Again, your actual numbers vary with user behavior.

[20:00] Devon: let's talk batching tradeoffs — when you increase the batch window from 12ms to 30ms what did that do to throughput and tail latency?
[20:07] Priya: we ran an A/B: 12ms had 13 tps and p95 of 0.42s for typical short prompts; 30ms increased throughput to 17 tps but p95 moved to ~0.61s in that scenario. For longer prompts the benefit is larger — more consolidation yields better GPU efficiency. If you can tolerate p95 up to ~600ms for certain flows, value per dollar improves substantially.

[22:30] Marta: can we do adaptive batching? Like low-latency routes keep 12ms and a background route switches to 30ms on different endpoint?
[22:36] Priya: yes, Redwood runtime supports configurable routes with separate batch windows; you can set route-level policies and we can provision separate GPU pools or share with QoS. That's exactly what we'd recommend for mixed workloads.

[24:44] Neil: about the KV cache retention test you proposed — what's the parameter set?
[24:50] Priya: plan: run a 2-hour retention sweep across three retention settings: 15min, 60min, and 240min. We'll measure hit-rate, tokens/sec, and memory pressure. We'll also collect request-level histograms so you can map to user sessions. Expect artifacts: a CSV per run and a short notebook with charts.
[25:15] Devon: memory pressure is critical, our infra team needs to know the size impact; if retention is too long it'll push up GPU memory or require an external memcache.
[25:24] Priya: agreed — we'll include estimated memory usage and fallback to external Redis if needed; Redwood supports in-node KV vs external. We'll note tradeoffs in the report.

[27:05] Marta: a scenario: if a wrong prefix match occurs it might return inconsistent summaries — do you have config to prefer conservative cache checks?
[27:12] Priya: yes, we support strict prefix matching and optional similarity thresholds; you can enable conservative mode to reduce false-positive hits at the expense of hit-rate. We'll include a small matrix of quality vs hit-rate from the replay.

[29:30] Jordan: question for Axion — what's your expected 90-day traffic pattern once you go full prod? Are you planning 24/7 steady or spiky daytime?
[29:38] Marta: mostly spiky—peaks during business hours and batched nightly processing for analytics. We expect daily peaks to be roughly 4x baseline.

[31:02] Priya: okay that helps. For spiky workloads we recommend a mix of reserved dedicated pool for baseline and burst to hosted for peak — or vice versa depending on security. For now, pilot with reserved commit plus burst is the pragmatic path.

[33:10] Devon: any gotchas with autoscale and database connections? We had issues with too many ephemeral connections on scale events last month.
[33:18] Priya: autoscale events can create connection churn; we recommend connection pooling and graceful drain hooks. Redwood's Dedicated product has drain windows and backpressure to limit concurrency spikes. We'll share suggested infra patterns.

[35:45] Neil: a nit — in the bench you shared the tokens/sec/$ calculation uses a GPU amortized cost that included network egress. Could you re-run without egress to compare to our internal cost model?
[35:55] Jordan: sure, Jordan: action item — I'll update the spreadsheet and provide two views (with and without egress) and also include an apples-to-apples with your cloud rates.

[38:10] Marta: what's the rough expectation for improvement if we push caching from 48% to 65%?
[38:17] Priya: ballpark, improving hit-rate to 65% would reduce token generation by ~58% and could boost tokens/sec/$ by ~2.5-3x depending on baseline. We can model that with your actual session mix quickly once Devon provides the seq-length distribution.

[40:05] Devon: I'm worried about cold-starts when cache misses coincide with heavy load; does Redwood have graceful fallback to a smaller model to preserve latency?
[40:14] Priya: yes we support model variants and automatic fallback — you can configure a lower-cost smaller model as a fallback for time-critical endpoints. It trades off quality but keeps p95 bounded. We can demo fallback flows in the on-prem deep dive.

[42:30] Jordan: okay, let's capture explicit next steps. Priya will run KV retention tests. Devon will send sequence distribution. Jordan will update economics sheet and send SOW. We'll aim to reconvene next Tuesday with initial KV results.

[43:02] Marta: sounds good. Also, please include in the follow-up the logs showing when the kernel fallback path happened, that was interesting in the run where seqs > 1024.
[43:12] Priya: will do, I'll annotate the kernel fallback timestamps.

[45:20] Neil: procurement-wise once we have SOW and security docs we'll need a high-level runbook for on-prem install — what is the lead time?
[45:29] Jordan: for Private on-prem installs typical lead time is 6-8 weeks from signed SOW for the full package; we can do a faster air-gap proof-of-concept in ~2-3 weeks with a limited footprint. I'll include both timelines in the follow-up.

[47:50] Marta: any mention of competitive positioning? We briefly compared to CerebroAPI — their caching story is heavier on client-side embedding caches but their runtime didn't have the same quantization optimizations.
[48:03] Priya: yep, we also see LargeCloudAI offering good autoscale but less transparent unit economics. We'll keep showing the pilot numbers so you can make a direct call.

[50:30] Jordan: final quick recap: immediate engineering next steps are the 2-hour retention sweep, sequence-length export, and updated economics sheet. Business next steps: Jordan to send SOW and security docs. Schedule tech deep dive if retention test indicates memory bumps.

[51:12] Marta: one last thing — can you include a short example of how routing rules would look in config? We want to hand that to infra.
[51:20] Priya: yes, I'll include a config snippet and a small mapping doc.

[52:05] Jordan: great, thanks everyone. We'll capture action items in the follow-up email and target the check-in next Tuesday same time.
[52:14] Devon: thanks all.
[52:16] Marta: thanks.
[52:18] Neil: thanks, bye.

[52:30] End meeting."
